name: SpaceX

summary.text: SpaceX (Space Exploration Technologies Corp.) is a California launch and satellite company. Tesla's 2010 registration statement lists Elon Musk as its chief executive, chief technology officer and chairman since May 2002. NASA selected it, from a field of 20 applicants, in August 2006 for a funded Commercial Orbital Transportation Services Space Act Agreement; Commercial Resupply Services (2008) and Commercial Crew (2014, alongside Boeing) contracts followed. Founders Fund made a $20 million equity investment in 2008. Its Starlink satellite internet service has been used in Ukraine since 2022: USAID bought terminals from SpaceX in March 2022 and the Pentagon confirmed in June 2023 that it contracts with Starlink for Ukraine. Reuters reported in March 2024 that its Starshield unit holds a $1.8 billion contract, signed in 2021, with the National Reconnaissance Office.

facts.claim: On August 18, 2006 NASA announced that it had selected SpaceX of El Segundo, California, and Rocketplane-Kistler of Oklahoma City for Phase 1 of its Commercial Orbital Transportation Services (COTS) demonstration, signing Space Act Agreements with milestones and objective criteria. NASA said the two were chosen from 20 applicants; its COTS program office recorded 21 proposals from 20 companies and six semi-finalists (Andrews Space, Rocketplane-Kistler, SpaceDev, SpaceX, SPACEHAB and t/Space). NASA said it would buy crew and cargo services competitively in Phase 2 once a capability was demonstrated.
facts.quote: NASA and the two companies signed Space Act Agreements that establish milestones and objective criteria to assess their progress throughout Phase 1 of the competition.

facts.claim: Trade press reported the 2006 COTS Phase 1 awards as about $278 million for SpaceX and $207 million for Rocketplane Kistler, paid against development and flight milestones rather than as a conventional procurement contract; Flightglobal put the two companies' combined share at $485 million over four years, and Via Satellite, citing Defense Daily, described SpaceX's award as more than $270 million.
facts.quote: RpK was awarded a $207 million deal. The other winner was SpaceX, which was awarded the remaining $278 million.

facts.claim: NASA terminated Rocketplane Kistler's funded COTS agreement on October 18, 2007 after the company missed milestones, and in February 2008 selected Orbital Sciences Corporation as a replacement COTS partner. SpaceX's agreement continued.
facts.quote: On Thursday, October 18, 2007, NASA terminated its funded agreement with aerospace firm Rocketplane Kistler after the company missed milestones.

facts.claim: On December 23, 2008 NASA awarded fixed-price Commercial Resupply Services contracts for International Space Station cargo to two companies: 12 flights valued at about $1.6 billion to SpaceX and eight flights valued at about $1.9 billion to Orbital Sciences, each with a maximum potential value of about $3.1 billion.

facts.claim: On September 16, 2014 NASA selected both Boeing and SpaceX for firm fixed-price Commercial Crew Transportation Capability contracts, with maximum potential values of $4.2 billion (Boeing) and $2.6 billion (SpaceX), to carry NASA astronauts to the International Space Station.

sources.title: NASA Chooses American Companies to Transport U.S. Astronauts to International Space Station

facts.claim: The decision to retire the Space Shuttle predates NASA's commercial cargo and crew programs. On January 14, 2004 President George W. Bush announced the Vision for Space Exploration at NASA Headquarters; the White House fact sheet committed to completing the International Space Station by 2010, and the plan called for retiring the shuttle when station assembly was complete. NASA Administrator Sean O'Keefe told Congress that retiring the shuttle would free over $4 billion a year for lunar missions, and ending the shuttle also avoided the 2010 recertification called for by the Columbia Accident Investigation Board. The final shuttle mission, STS-135, flew in July 2011.
facts.quote: America will complete its work on the International Space Station by 2010, fulfilling our commitment to our 15 partner countries.

facts.claim: In August 2008 SpaceX received a $20 million equity investment from Founders Fund, a San Francisco venture firm run by Musk's fellow PayPal co-founders; Musk said in an August 4, 2008 statement that SpaceX welcomed managing partner Luke Nosek to its board. Musk had first told employees of an outside investment in an August 2 message sent shortly after a Falcon 1 launch failure.
facts.quote: SpaceX received a $20 million equity investment from Founders Fund, a San Francisco-based technology venture capital firm whose management team includes the co-founders of PayPal.

sources.title: PayPal Co-Founders Invest $20 Million in SpaceX
SpaceX Receives $20 Million Investment

facts.claim: In the first weeks of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, USAID bought 175 Starlink terminals from SpaceX on March 2, 2022 and 1,333 more on March 17, 2022, while SpaceX donated 3,667 terminals and the internet service; USAID announced the partnership as 5,000 terminals delivered to Ukraine. A 2025 USAID Inspector General inspection counted 5,175 terminals delivered to Ukraine's State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection.
facts.quote: SpaceX donated 3,667 terminals and the internet service itself, while USAID purchased the remaining 1,333 terminals.

sources.title: SpaceX and USAID deliver 5,000 Starlink internet terminals to Ukraine
Ukraine Response: USAID Did Not Fully Mitigate the Risk of Misuse of the Starlink Terminals Delivered to Ukraine (redacted final report)

facts.claim: USAID's Office of Inspector General found in 2025 that USAID did not fully mitigate the risk of misuse of the Starlink terminals it delivered to Ukraine, that nearly half of the active terminals were present in territory Russia fully or partially occupied, and that USAID said tracking the terminals once handed to Ukraine was impractical under wartime conditions.
facts.quote: nearly half of active terminals were present in territories that Russia fully or partially occupied

sources.title: Ukraine Response: USAID Did Not Fully Mitigate the Risk of Misuse of the Starlink Terminals Delivered to Ukraine (redacted final report)
Half of Starlink terminals sent to Ukraine found in Russian-occupied areas, US agency says

facts.claim: On June 1, 2023 the Pentagon confirmed that it had contracted with SpaceX for Starlink services for Ukraine, after Bloomberg first reported the contract; it declined to disclose the cost, timing or length of service, citing operational security. SpaceX had said in September 2022 that it could not continue paying for Starlink service in Ukraine and had asked the Pentagon to cover the costs.
facts.quote: Satellite communications constitute a vital layer in Ukraine's overall communications network and the department contracts with Starlink for services of this type.

sources.title: Pentagon confirms SpaceX deal for Ukraine Starlink services
Pentagon says it's paying for Elon Musk's Starlink internet in Ukraine
Pentagon awards SpaceX with Ukraine contract for Starlink satellite internet

facts.claim: Walter Isaacson's 2023 biography of Musk, in an excerpt first reported by CNN, said that in September 2022 Musk secretly told SpaceX engineers to turn off Starlink coverage within 100 kilometers of the Crimean coast, so that Ukrainian drone submarines approaching the Russian fleet at Sevastopol lost connectivity and washed ashore; Isaacson attributed the decision to Musk's fear that Russia would respond to an attack on Crimea with nuclear weapons.
facts.quote: secretly told his engineers to turn off coverage within 100 kilometers of the Crimean coast

sources.title: Elon Musk says he denied Ukraine satellite request to avoid complicity in "major act of war" vs. Russia
Musk says he prevented Ukraine from launching attack on Russian ships (Starlink/Crimea)
Starlink: Ukraine spy chief says satellite system in use on 'all front lines,' but wasn't active 'for time' over Crimea

facts.claim: Responding to the Isaacson excerpt, Musk posted on X in September 2023 that 'The Starlink regions in question were not activated. SpaceX did not deactivate anything,' that 'There was an emergency request from government authorities to activate Starlink all the way to Sevastopol,' and that complying would have made SpaceX 'explicitly complicit in a major act of war and conflict escalation.'
facts.quote: The Starlink regions in question were not activated. SpaceX did not deactivate anything.

sources.title: Elon Musk says he denied Ukraine satellite request to avoid complicity in "major act of war" vs. Russia
Musk says he prevented Ukraine from launching attack on Russian ships (Starlink/Crimea)

facts.claim: CNN reported on September 11, 2023 that Isaacson was walking back the claim that Musk had ordered Starlink coverage near Crimea turned off, saying the claim 'turned out not to be quite as Isaacson had told it.' CNN separately reported that Ukraine's military intelligence chief said Starlink was in use on all front lines but had not been active over Crimea for a time.
facts.quote: the explosive claim turned out not to be quite as Isaacson had told it

sources.title: An explosive Elon Musk biography is just hitting shelves. But the book's acclaimed author is already walking back a major claim
Starlink: Ukraine spy chief says satellite system in use on 'all front lines,' but wasn't active 'for time' over Crimea

facts.claim: Reuters reported on March 17, 2024, citing five unnamed sources, that SpaceX's Starshield unit is building a network of hundreds of Earth-imaging satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office under a $1.8 billion contract signed in 2021; the Wall Street Journal had reported the classified $1.8 billion contract in February 2024 without naming the agency. SpaceX did not respond to Reuters, the Pentagon referred questions to the NRO and SpaceX, and the NRO declined to comment on the extent of SpaceX's role.
facts.quote: The work is done by SpaceX's Starshield unit under a $1.8 billion deal from 2021 with the National Reconnaissance Office, the agency that runs U.S. spy satellites.

facts.claim: Musk's ownership of SpaceX has been reported at about 42% before the company's February 2026 acquisition of xAI (Forbes, December 2025, when a tender offer valued his stake; another report put his pre-merger holding at about 42% of the equity and 80% of the votes, citing FCC filings), an estimated 43% after the xAI merger (CNBC, February 2026), roughly 40% after the June 2026 initial public offering (Bloomberg), and 38% including options in Forbes's profile as of September 2026. CNBC reported from the IPO filings that Musk would hold 82.4% of the voting power after the market debut.
facts.quote: founder and CEO Elon Musk will have voting control of 82.4% in SpaceX, according to the company's IPO filings

facts.claim: On February 2, 2004 NASA issued a pre-solicitation notice for a non-competed contract with Kistler Aerospace to help demonstrate a commercial launch system's ability to resupply the International Space Station (reported at $277 million by Citizens Against Government Waste, $227 million by the Center for Growth and Opportunity and $234 million by Space.com). SpaceX protested the sole-source award to the General Accounting Office the following month, and NASA withdrew the notice in 2004 before any GAO ruling; Space.com reported in 2005 that NASA rescinded the award after GAO indicated it would likely rule for SpaceX.
facts.quote: following protests filed with the General Accounting Office (GAO), NASA yanked the notice

sources.title: NASA Yanks Sole-Source Contract After GAO Protest

sources.publisher: The Center for Growth and Opportunity at Utah State University
sources.title: A 2006 NASA program shows how government can move at the speed of startups
SpaceX Fighting for USAF Launches

facts.claim: On December 19, 2006 the Government Accountability Office dismissed a protest by Exploration Partners, LLC (B-298804) against NASA's issuance of funded Space Act agreements to SpaceX and Rocketplane Kistler under COTS announcement COTS-01-05. GAO held that NASA's use of its 'other transactions' authority under the Space Act is not tantamount to the award of procurement contracts subject to GAO's bid-protest jurisdiction; six firms including SpaceX and Rocketplane had been invited to negotiations and the protester had not.
facts.quote: is not tantamount to the award of contracts for the procurement of goods and services, which would be subject to our bid protest jurisdiction

sources.title: Exploration Partners, LLC, B-298804
Decision, Exploration Partners, LLC, B-298804 (PDF)

facts.claim: In early 2008 the GAO denied a protest by Rocketplane Kistler (B-310741), which had argued that NASA was required to acquire the COTS work through a procurement contract rather than a Space Act agreement; the decision notes that Rocketplane and SpaceX had received Space Act agreements supporting phase 1 of the COTS project.

sources.title: Rocketplane Kistler, B-310741
GAO Rejects Rocketplane Kistler Protest On Losing NASA Funding

openQuestions: The brief's claim that Errol Musk's Zambian emerald dealings were used to bypass South African exchange controls: no source retrieved this session (News24, MyBroadband, Business Insider via Yahoo, InsideHook) mentions exchange controls or capital flight. Errol Musk's own account, via Isaacson, is that raw emeralds were imported into South Africa and cut in Johannesburg, and that he sold them to jewellers on overseas trips in a 'cloak and dagger thing, because none of it was legal'. Which law he meant is not stated. See research/findings/errol-musk.json.

COTS total paid to SpaceX ($396 million for 40 milestones, per NASA's 2013 lessons-learned document) is recorded in research/handoffs/nasa-cots-spacex.json; the CRS 2008 and Commercial Crew 2014 facts above reuse that record's sources, which were not re-opened this session.

Pentagon Starlink-for-Ukraine contract: value and duration were not disclosed. A reported September 2023 U.S. Space Force Starshield contract (about $70 million) and Reuters' own page on the NRO contract were not retrieved; the SCMP and Asia Financial republications are cited instead.
Crimea 2022: Isaacson's exact clarification wording was cut off in the CNN text retrieved; Musk's X posts were seen only as quoted by CBS and NBC.
The CRS (2008) and Commercial Crew (2014) facts cite the same sources as the approved handoff records nasa-cots-spacex and shuttle-commercial-crew rather than pages opened for this file.

Musk's $100 million founding investment is now sourced to CNBC (2020); SpaceX's own 2026 IPO prospectus was not opened for the founding capital or for the stake figures, which vary by date and by whether options are counted (42% December 2025; 43% after the February 2026 xAI merger; about 40% after the June 2026 IPO; 38% per Forbes, September 2026). The statement that Musk held about 42% of the equity and 80% of the votes before the xAI deal 'according to FCC reports' was returned without its source being identified among the results (Fortune, May 2026, is the likeliest).

The 'sole-source' question: NASA's COTS, CRS and Commercial Crew awards were competed (NASA's 2006 release names 20 applicants; CRS and Commercial Crew went to two companies each). The only sole-source episode found is NASA's February 2004 pre-solicitation notice to Kistler, which SpaceX protested and NASA withdrew in 2004. No GAO decision on that 2004 protest was found on gao.gov (the docket number is unconfirmed; NASA withdrew before a ruling, per CAGW, the CGO and Space.com), and the contract value is given as $277 million (CAGW), $227 million (CGO) or $234 million (Space.com). Space.com's 'rare protest victory' and its statement that GAO had indicated it would likely rule for SpaceX were returned in a search summary and should be confirmed in the article. The GAO decisions that were found (B-298804, 2006; B-310741, 2008) concern later protests by other parties and hold that Space Act agreements are outside GAO's bid-protest jurisdiction.
